abstract: Organismal traits play a distinct role in shaping community assembly, yet they have received comparatively little attention in marine communities. Here, we focus on living benthic foraminifera, a diverse group of marine protists that inhabit the seafloor. Benthic foraminifera are protists that have evolved different test-construction strategies: either by selecting and agglutinating grains from their surrounding environment or by biomineralization. In addition, taxa exhibit distinct morphologies have been hypothesized to reflect microhabitat partitioning within sediments. Here, we investigate their metacommunity patterns by analysing a co-occurrence network covering the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. We found that test-construction strategies significantly explained the structure of the network, whereas the general test shape did not. We hypothesize that test-construction strategy act as a broader-scale filter on the regional species pool, whereas morphological differences may be more closely related to local-scale coexistence and habitat partitioning. This study supports the idea that different organismal traits have different roles in the community assembly process.
